1: //! Rewriting strategies for circuit optimisation.
2: //!
3: //! This module contains the [`RewriteStrategy`] trait, which is currently
4: //! implemented by
5: //! - [`GreedyRewriteStrategy`], which applies as many rewrites as possible on
6: //!   one circuit, and
7: //! - Exhaustive strategies, which clone the original circuit and explore every
8: //!   possible rewrite (with some pruning strategy):
9: //!    - [`ExhaustiveGreedyStrategy`], which applies multiple combinations of
10: //!      non-overlapping rewrites.
11: //!    - [`ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy`], which tries every rewrite below
12: //!      threshold function.
13: //!
14: //! The exhaustive strategies are parametrised by a strategy cost function:
15: //!    - [`LexicographicCostFunction`] allows rewrites that do
16: //!      not increase some coarse cost function (e.g. CX count), whilst
17: //!      ordering them according to a lexicographic ordering of finer cost
18: //!      functions (e.g. total gate count). See
19: //!      [`LexicographicCostFunction::default_cx`]) for a default implementation.
20: //!    - [`GammaStrategyCost`] ignores rewrites that increase the cost
21: //!      function beyond a percentage given by a f64 parameter gamma.
22: 
23: use std::{collections::HashSet, fmt::Debug};
24: 
25: use derive_more::From;
26: use hugr::ops::OpType;
27: use hugr::Hugr;
28: use itertools::Itertools;
29: 
30: use crate::circuit::cost::{is_cx, is_quantum, CircuitCost, CostDelta, LexicographicCost};
31: use crate::Circuit;
32: 
33: use super::trace::{RewriteTrace, RewriteTracer};
34: use super::CircuitRewrite;
35: 
36: /// Rewriting strategies for circuit optimisation.
37: ///
38: /// A rewrite strategy takes a set of possible rewrites and applies them
39: /// to a circuit according to a strategy. It yields new circuits, each obtained
40: /// by applying one or several non-overlapping rewrites to the original
41: /// circuit.
42: ///
43: /// It also assign every circuit a totally ordered cost that can be used when
44: /// using rewrites for circuit optimisation.
45: pub trait RewriteStrategy {
46:     /// The circuit cost to be minimised.
47:     type Cost: CircuitCost;
48: 
49:     /// Apply a set of rewrites to a circuit.
50:     ///
51:     /// Returns a lazy iterator of `(circuit, cost_delta)` pairs for each
52:     /// rewritten circuit, so consumers can process candidates on demand and
53:     /// skip generating the rest when they don't need them.
54:     fn apply_rewrites<'a>(
55:         &'a self,
56:         rewrites: impl IntoIterator<Item = CircuitRewrite> + 'a,
57:         circ: &'a Hugr,
58:     ) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Hugr, <Self::Cost as CircuitCost>::CostDelta)> + 'a;
59: 
60:     /// The cost of a single operation for this strategy's cost function.
61:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::Cost;
62: 
63:     /// The cost of a circuit using this strategy's cost function.
64:     #[inline]
65:     fn circuit_cost(&self, circ: &Hugr) -> Self::Cost {
66:         circ.circuit_cost(|op| self.op_cost(op))
67:     }
68: 
69:     /// Returns the cost of a rewrite's matched subcircuit before replacing it.
70:     #[inline]
71:     fn pre_rewrite_cost(&self, rw: &CircuitRewrite, circ: &Hugr) -> Self::Cost {
72:         circ.nodes_cost(rw.subcircuit().nodes().iter().copied(), |op| {
73:             self.op_cost(op)
74:         })
75:     }
76: 
77:     /// Returns the expected cost of a rewrite's matched subcircuit after replacing it.
78:     fn post_rewrite_cost(&self, rw: &CircuitRewrite) -> Self::Cost {
79:         rw.replacement().circuit_cost(|op| self.op_cost(op))
80:     }
81: }
82: 
83: /// A rewrite strategy applying as many non-overlapping rewrites as possible.
84: ///
85: /// All possible rewrites are sorted by the number of gates they remove from
86: /// the circuit and are applied in order. If a rewrite overlaps with a rewrite
87: /// that has already been applied, it is skipped.
88: ///
89: /// This strategy will always return exactly one circuit: the original circuit
90: /// with as many rewrites applied as possible.
91: ///
92: /// Rewrites are only applied if they strictly decrease gate count.
93: #[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
94: pub struct GreedyRewriteStrategy;
95: 
96: impl RewriteStrategy for GreedyRewriteStrategy {
97:     type Cost = usize;
98: 
99:     #[tracing::instrument(skip_all)]
100:     fn apply_rewrites<'a>(
101:         &'a self,
102:         rewrites: impl IntoIterator<Item = CircuitRewrite> + 'a,
103:         circ: &'a Hugr,
104:     ) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Hugr, isize)> + 'a {
105:         let rewrites = rewrites
106:             .into_iter()
107:             .sorted_by_key(|rw| rw.node_count_delta())
108:             .take_while(|rw| rw.node_count_delta() < 0);
109:         let mut changed_nodes = HashSet::new();
110:         let mut cost_delta = 0;
111:         let mut circ = circ.clone();
112:         for rewrite in rewrites {
113:             if rewrite
114:                 .subcircuit()
115:                 .nodes()
116:                 .iter()
117:                 .any(|n| changed_nodes.contains(n))
118:             {
119:                 continue;
120:             }
121:             changed_nodes.extend(rewrite.subcircuit().nodes().iter().copied());
122:             cost_delta += rewrite.node_count_delta();
123:             rewrite
124:                 .apply(&mut circ)
125:                 .expect("Could not perform rewrite in greedy strategy");
126:         }
127:         std::iter::once((circ, cost_delta))
128:     }
129: 
130:     fn circuit_cost(&self, circ: &Hugr) -> Self::Cost {
131:         circ.num_gates()
132:     }
133: 
134:     fn op_cost(&self, _op: &OpType) -> Self::Cost {
135:         1
136:     }
137: }
138: 
139: /// Exhaustive strategies based on cost functions and thresholds.
140: ///
141: /// Every possible rewrite is applied to a copy of the input circuit. In
142: /// addition, other non-overlapping rewrites are applied greedily in ascending
143: /// cost delta.
144: ///
145: /// Thus for one circuit, up to `n` rewritten circuits will be returned, each
146: /// obtained by applying at least one of the `n` rewrites to the original
147: /// circuit.
148: ///
149: /// Whether a rewrite is allowed or not is determined by a cost function and a
150: /// threshold function: if the cost of the target of the rewrite is below the
151: /// threshold given by the cost of the original circuit, the rewrite is
152: /// performed.
153: ///
154: /// The cost function must return a value of type `Self::OpCost`. All op costs
155: /// are summed up to obtain a total cost that is then compared using the
156: /// threshold function.
157: ///
158: /// This kind of strategy is not recommended for thresholds that allow positive
159: /// cost deltas, as these will always be greedily applied even if they increase
160: /// the final cost.
161: #[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone, From)]
162: pub struct ExhaustiveGreedyStrategy<T> {
163:     /// The cost function.
164:     pub strat_cost: T,
165: }
166: 
167: impl<T: StrategyCost> RewriteStrategy for ExhaustiveGreedyStrategy<T> {
168:     type Cost = T::OpCost;
169: 
170:     #[tracing::instrument(skip_all)]
171:     fn apply_rewrites<'a>(
172:         &'a self,
173:         rewrites: impl IntoIterator<Item = CircuitRewrite> + 'a,
174:         circ: &'a Hugr,
175:     ) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Hugr, <T::OpCost as CircuitCost>::CostDelta)> + 'a {
176:         // Check only the rewrites that reduce the size of the circuit.
177:         let rewrites = rewrites
178:             .into_iter()
179:             .filter_map(|rw| {
180:                 let pattern_cost = self.pre_rewrite_cost(&rw, circ);
181:                 let target_cost = self.post_rewrite_cost(&rw);
182:                 if !self.strat_cost.under_threshold(&pattern_cost, &target_cost) {
183:                     return None;
184:                 }
185:                 Some((rw, target_cost.sub_cost(&pattern_cost)))
186:             })
187:             .sorted_by_key(|(_, delta)| delta.clone())
188:             .collect_vec();
189: 
190:         (0..rewrites.len()).map(move |i| {
191:             let mut curr_circ = circ.clone();
192:             let mut changed_nodes = HashSet::new();
193:             let mut cost_delta = Default::default();
194:             let mut composed_rewrite_count = 0;
195:             for (rewrite, delta) in &rewrites[i..] {
196:                 if !changed_nodes.is_empty()
197:                     && rewrite
198:                         .invalidation_set()
199:                         .any(|n| changed_nodes.contains(&n))
200:                 {
201:                     continue;
202:                 }
203:                 changed_nodes.extend(rewrite.invalidation_set());
204:                 cost_delta += delta.clone();
205: 
206:                 composed_rewrite_count += 1;
207: 
208:                 rewrite
209:                     .clone()
210:                     .apply_notrace(&mut curr_circ)
211:                     .expect("Could not perform rewrite in exhaustive greedy strategy");
212:             }
213: 
214:             curr_circ.add_rewrite_trace(RewriteTrace::new(composed_rewrite_count));
215:             (curr_circ, cost_delta)
216:         })
217:     }
218: 
219:     #[inline]
220:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::Cost {
221:         self.strat_cost.op_cost(op)
222:     }
223: }
224: 
225: /// Exhaustive strategies based on cost functions and thresholds.
226: ///
227: /// Every possible rewrite is applied to a copy of the input circuit. Thus for
228: /// one circuit, up to `n` rewritten circuits will be returned, each obtained
229: /// by applying one of the `n` rewrites to the original circuit.
230: ///
231: /// Whether a rewrite is allowed or not is determined by a cost function and a
232: /// threshold function: if the cost of the target of the rewrite is below the
233: /// threshold given by the cost of the original circuit, the rewrite is
234: /// performed.
235: ///
236: /// The cost function must return a value of type `Self::OpCost`. All op costs
237: /// are summed up to obtain a total cost that is then compared using the
238: /// threshold function.
239: #[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone, From)]
240: pub struct ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<T> {
241:     /// The cost function.
242:     pub strat_cost: T,
243: }
244: 
245: impl<T: StrategyCost> RewriteStrategy for ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<T> {
246:     type Cost = T::OpCost;
247: 
248:     #[tracing::instrument(skip_all)]
249:     fn apply_rewrites<'a>(
250:         &'a self,
251:         rewrites: impl IntoIterator<Item = CircuitRewrite> + 'a,
252:         circ: &'a Hugr,
253:     ) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Hugr, <T::OpCost as CircuitCost>::CostDelta)> + 'a {
254:         rewrites.into_iter().filter_map(|rw| {
255:             let pattern_cost = self.pre_rewrite_cost(&rw, circ);
256:             let target_cost = self.post_rewrite_cost(&rw);
257:             if !self.strat_cost.under_threshold(&pattern_cost, &target_cost) {
258:                 return None;
259:             }
260:             let mut circ = circ.clone();
261:             rw.apply(&mut circ).expect("invalid pattern match");
262:             Some((circ, target_cost.sub_cost(&pattern_cost)))
263:         })
264:     }
265: 
266:     #[inline]
267:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::Cost {
268:         self.strat_cost.op_cost(op)
269:     }
270: }
271: 
272: /// Cost function definitions required in exhaustive strategies.
273: ///
274: /// See [`ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy`], [`ExhaustiveGreedyStrategy`].
275: pub trait StrategyCost {
276:     /// The cost of a single operation.
277:     type OpCost: CircuitCost;
278: 
279:     /// Returns true if the rewrite is allowed, based on the cost of the pattern and target.
280:     #[inline]
281:     fn under_threshold(&self, pattern_cost: &Self::OpCost, target_cost: &Self::OpCost) -> bool {
282:         target_cost.sub_cost(pattern_cost).as_isize() <= 0
283:     }
284: 
285:     /// The cost of a single operation.
286:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::OpCost;
287: }
288: 
289: /// Rewrite strategy cost allowing smaller or equal cost rewrites.
290: ///
291: /// Rewrites are permitted based on a coarse cost function: if
292: /// the coarse cost of the target of the rewrite is smaller or equal to the
293: /// coarse cost of the pattern, the rewrite is allowed.
294: ///
295: /// Further more fine-grained cost functions can be used as tie breakers: within
296: /// circuits with the same coarse cost, circuits are ranked according to a
297: /// lexicographic ordering of their cost functions.
298: ///
299: /// An example would be to use the number of CX gates as coarse cost and the
300: /// total number of gates as the only fine grained cost function.
301: ///
302: /// Lexicographic orderings may be useful to add relief to an otherwise flat
303: /// optimisation landscape.
304: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
305: pub struct LexicographicCostFunction<F, const N: usize> {
306:     cost_fns: [F; N],
307: }
308: 
309: impl<F, const N: usize> StrategyCost for LexicographicCostFunction<F, N>
310: where
311:     F: Fn(&OpType) -> usize,
312: {
313:     type OpCost = LexicographicCost<usize, N>;
314: 
315:     #[inline]
316:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::OpCost {
317:         let mut costs = [0; N];
318:         for (cost_fn, cost_mut) in self.cost_fns.iter().zip(&mut costs) {
319:             *cost_mut = cost_fn(op);
320:         }
321:         costs.into()
322:     }
323: }
324: 
325: impl LexicographicCostFunction<fn(&OpType) -> usize, 2> {
326:     /// Non-increasing rewrite strategy based on CX count.
327:     ///
328:     /// A fine-grained cost function given by the total number of quantum gates
329:     /// is used to rank circuits with equal CX count.
330:     ///
331:     /// This is probably a good default for NISQ-y circuit optimisation.
332:     #[inline]
333:     pub fn default_cx() -> ExhaustiveGreedyStrategy<Self> {
334:         Self {
335:             cost_fns: [|op| is_cx(op) as usize, |op| is_quantum(op) as usize],
336:         }
337:         .into()
338:     }
339: }
340: 
341: /// Rewrite strategy cost allowing rewrites with bounded cost increase.
342: ///
343: /// The parameter gamma controls how greedy the algorithm should be. It allows a
344: /// rewrite C1 -> C2 if C2 has at most gamma times the cost of C1:
345: ///
346: /// $cost(C2) < gamma * cost(C1)$
347: ///
348: /// The cost function is given by the sum of the cost of each operation in the
349: /// circuit. This allows for instance to use of the total number of gates (true
350: /// predicate), the number of CX gates or a weighted sum of gate types as cost
351: /// functions.
352: ///
353: /// gamma = 1 is the greedy strategy where a rewrite is only allowed if it
354: /// strictly reduces the gate count. The default is gamma = 1.0001 (as set in
355: /// the Quartz paper) and the number of CX gates. This essentially allows
356: /// rewrites that improve or leave the number of CX unchanged.
357: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
358: pub struct GammaStrategyCost<C> {
359:     /// The gamma parameter.
360:     pub gamma: f64,
361:     /// A cost function for each operation.
362:     pub op_cost: C,
363: }
364: 
365: impl<C: Fn(&OpType) -> usize> StrategyCost for GammaStrategyCost<C> {
366:     type OpCost = usize;
367: 
368:     #[inline]
369:     fn under_threshold(&self, &pattern_cost: &Self::OpCost, &target_cost: &Self::OpCost) -> bool {
370:         (target_cost as f64) < self.gamma * (pattern_cost as f64)
371:     }
372: 
373:     #[inline]
374:     fn op_cost(&self, op: &OpType) -> Self::OpCost {
375:         (self.op_cost)(op)
376:     }
377: }
378: 
379: impl<C> GammaStrategyCost<C> {
380:     /// New exhaustive rewrite strategy with provided predicate.
381:     ///
382:     /// The gamma parameter is set to the default 1.0001.
383:     #[inline]
384:     pub fn with_cost(op_cost: C) -> ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<Self> {
385:         Self {
386:             gamma: 1.0001,
387:             op_cost,
388:         }
389:         .into()
390:     }
391: 
392:     /// New exhaustive rewrite strategy with provided gamma and predicate.
393:     #[inline]
394:     pub fn new(gamma: f64, op_cost: C) -> ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<Self> {
395:         Self { gamma, op_cost }.into()
396:     }
397: }
398: 
399: impl GammaStrategyCost<fn(&OpType) -> usize> {
400:     /// Exhaustive rewrite strategy with CX count cost function.
401:     ///
402:     /// The gamma parameter is set to the default 1.0001. This is a good default
403:     /// choice for NISQ-y circuits, where CX gates are the most expensive.
404:     #[inline]
405:     pub fn exhaustive_cx() -> ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<Self> {
406:         GammaStrategyCost::with_cost(|op| is_cx(op) as usize)
407:     }
408: 
409:     /// Exhaustive rewrite strategy with CX count cost function and provided gamma.
410:     #[inline]
411:     pub fn exhaustive_cx_with_gamma(gamma: f64) -> ExhaustiveThresholdStrategy<Self> {
412:         GammaStrategyCost::new(gamma, |op| is_cx(op) as usize)
413:     }
414: }

416: #[cfg(test)]

37:         hugr: &Hugr,

51:     }

54:     pub fn create_rewrite(
55:         &self,
56:         source: &Hugr,
57:         target: Hugr,
58:     ) -> Result<CircuitRewrite, InvalidReplacement> {

71:     pub fn try_new(
72:         source_position: &Subcircuit,
73:         source: &Hugr,
74:         target: Hugr,
75:     ) -> Result<Self, InvalidReplacement> {
76:         source_position
77:             .subgraph

80:     }

85:     /// number is an increase in node count, a negative number is a decrease.
86:     pub fn node_count_delta(&self) -> isize {
87:         let new_count = self.replacement().num_gates() as isize;
88:         let old_count = self.subcircuit().node_count() as isize;
89:         new_count - old_count
90:     }

22: /// An edge property in a circuit pattern.
23: ///
24: /// Edges are
25: /// Edges are reversible if the edge type is linear.
26: #[derive(
27:     Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize,
28: )]
29: enum PEdge {
30:     /// A "normal" edge between src and dst within a pattern.
31:     InternalEdge {
32:         src: Port,
33:         dst: Port,
34:         is_reversible: bool,
35:     },
36:     /// An edge from a copied input to src.
37:     ///
38:     /// Edges from inputs are typically not matched as part of the pattern,
39:     /// unless a single input is copied multiple times. In this case, an
40:     /// InputEdge is used to link the source port to the (usually hidden)
41:     /// copy node.
42:     ///
43:     /// Input edges are always irreversible.
44:     InputEdge { src: Port },
45: }
46: 
47: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Error)]
48: enum InvalidEdgeProperty {
49:     /// The port is linked to multiple edges.
50:     #[error("port {0:?} is linked to multiple edges")]
51:     AmbiguousEdge(Port),
52:     /// The port is not linked to any edge.
53:     #[error("port {0:?} is not linked to any edge")]
54:     NoLinkedEdge(Port),
55:     /// The port does not have a type.
56:     #[error("port {0:?} does not have a type")]
57:     UntypedPort(Port),
58: }
59: 
60: impl PEdge {
61:     fn try_from_port(
62:         node: Node,
63:         port: Port,
64:         circ: &impl Circuit,
65:     ) -> Result<Self, InvalidEdgeProperty> {
66:         let src = port;
67:         let (dst_node, dst) = circ
68:             .linked_ports(node, src)
69:             .exactly_one()
70:             .map_err(|mut e| {
71:                 if e.next().is_some() {
72:                     InvalidEdgeProperty::AmbiguousEdge(src)
73:                 } else {
74:                     InvalidEdgeProperty::NoLinkedEdge(src)
75:                 }
76:             })?;
77:         if circ.get_optype(dst_node).tag() == OpTag::Input {
78:             return Ok(Self::InputEdge { src });
79:         }
80:         let port_type = circ
81:             .signature(node)
82:             .unwrap()
83:             .port_type(src)
84:             .cloned()
85:             .ok_or(InvalidEdgeProperty::UntypedPort(src))?;
86:         let is_reversible = type_is_linear(&port_type);
87:         Ok(Self::InternalEdge {
88:             src,
89:             dst,
90:             is_reversible,
91:         })
92:     }
93: }

99:         match *self {
100:             Self::InternalEdge {
101:                 src,
102:                 dst,
103:                 is_reversible,
104:             } => is_reversible.then_some(Self::InternalEdge {
105:                 src: dst,
106:                 dst: src,
107:                 is_reversible,
108:             }),
109:             Self::InputEdge { .. } => None,
110:         }
111:     }
112: 
113:     fn offset_id(&self) -> Self::OffsetID {
114:         match *self {
115:             Self::InternalEdge { src, .. } => src,
116:             Self::InputEdge { src, .. } => src,
117:         }

2: //! going between `tket_json_rs::optype::OpType` and `hugr::ops::OpType`.
3: //!
4: //! The `JsonOp` tries to homogenize the
5: //! `tket_json_rs::circuit_json::Operation`s coming from the encoded TKET1
6: //! circuits by ensuring they always define a signature, and computing the
7: //! explicit count of qubits and linear bits.

24: /// A serialized operation, containing the operation type and all its attributes.
25: ///
26: /// Wrapper around [`circuit_json::Operation`] with cached number of qubits and bits.
27: ///
28: /// The `Operation` contained by this struct is guaranteed to have a signature.
29: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
30: pub(crate) struct JsonOp {
31:     op: circuit_json::Operation,
32:     num_qubits: usize,
33:     num_bits: usize,
34:     /// Node input for each parameter in `op.params`.
35:     ///
36:     /// If the input is `None`, the parameter does not use a Hugr port and is
37:     /// instead stored purely as metadata for the `Operation`.
38:     param_inputs: Vec<Option<usize>>,
39:     /// The number of non-None inputs in `param_inputs`, corresponding to the
40:     /// FLOAT64_TYPE inputs to the Hugr operation.
41:     num_params: usize,
42: }
43: 
44: impl JsonOp {
45:     /// Create a new `JsonOp` from a `circuit_json::Operation`, computing its
46:     /// number of qubits from the signature
47:     ///
48:     /// Fails if the operation does not define a signature. See
49:     /// [`JsonOp::new_from_op`] for a version that generates a signature if none
50:     /// is defined.
51:     #[allow(unused)]
52:     pub fn new(op: circuit_json::Operation) -> Option<Self> {
53:         let Some(sig) = &op.signature else {
54:             return None;
55:         };
56:         let input_counts = sig.iter().map(String::as_ref).counts();
57:         let num_qubits = input_counts.get("Q").copied().unwrap_or(0);
58:         let num_bits = input_counts.get("B").copied().unwrap_or(0);
59:         let mut op = Self {
60:             op,
61:             num_qubits,
62:             num_bits,
63:             param_inputs: Vec::new(),
64:             num_params: 0,
65:         };
66:         op.compute_param_fields();
67:         Some(op)
68:     }
69: 
70:     /// Create a new `JsonOp` from a `circuit_json::Operation`, with the number
71:     /// of qubits and bits explicitly specified.
72:     ///
73:     /// If the operation does not define a signature, one is generated with the
74:     /// given amounts.
75:     pub fn new_from_op(
76:         mut op: circuit_json::Operation,
77:         num_qubits: usize,
78:         num_bits: usize,
79:     ) -> Self {
80:         if op.signature.is_none() {
81:             op.signature =
82:                 Some([vec!["Q".into(); num_qubits], vec!["B".into(); num_bits]].concat());
83:         }
84:         let mut op = Self {
85:             op,
86:             num_qubits,
87:             num_bits,
88:             param_inputs: Vec::new(),
89:             num_params: 0,
90:         };
91:         op.compute_param_fields();
92:         op
93:     }
94: 
95:     /// Create a new `JsonOp` from the optype and the number of parameters.
96:     pub fn new_with_counts(
97:         json_optype: JsonOpType,
98:         num_qubits: usize,
99:         num_bits: usize,
100:         num_params: usize,
101:     ) -> Self {
102:         let mut params = None;
103:         let mut param_inputs = vec![];
104:         if num_params > 0 {
105:             let offset = num_qubits + num_bits;
106:             params = Some(vec!["".into(); num_params]);
107:             param_inputs = (offset..offset + num_params).map(Option::Some).collect();
108:         }
109:         let op = circuit_json::Operation {
110:             op_type: json_optype,
111:             n_qb: Some(num_qubits as u32),
112:             params,
113:             op_box: None,
114:             signature: Some([vec!["Q".into(); num_qubits], vec!["B".into(); num_bits]].concat()),
115:             conditional: None,
116:         };
117:         Self {
118:             op,
119:             num_qubits,
120:             num_bits,
121:             param_inputs,
122:             num_params,
123:         }
124:     }
125: 
126:     /// Compute the signature of the operation.
127:     #[inline]
128:     pub fn signature(&self) -> FunctionType {
129:         let linear = [
130:             vec![QB_T; self.num_qubits],
131:             vec![LINEAR_BIT.clone(); self.num_bits],
132:         ]
133:         .concat();
134:         let params = vec![FLOAT64_TYPE; self.num_params];
135:         FunctionType::new([linear.clone(), params].concat(), linear)
136:         // .with_extension_delta(&ExtensionSet::singleton(&TKET1_EXTENSION_ID))
137:     }
138: 
139:     /// List of parameters in the operation that should be exposed as inputs.
140:     #[inline]
141:     pub fn param_inputs(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &str> {
142:         self.param_inputs
143:             .iter()
144:             .filter_map(|&i| self.op.params.as_ref()?.get(i?).map(String::as_ref))
145:     }
146: 
147:     pub fn into_operation(self) -> circuit_json::Operation {
148:         self.op
149:     }
150: 
151:     /// Wraps the op into a Hugr opaque operation
152:     fn as_opaque_op(&self) -> ExternalOp {
153:         crate::extension::wrap_json_op(self)
154:     }
155: 
156:     /// Compute the `parameter_input` and `num_params` fields by looking for
157:     /// parameters in `op.params` that can be mapped to input wires in the Hugr.
158:     ///
159:     /// Updates the internal `num_params` and `param_inputs` fields.
160:     fn compute_param_fields(&mut self) {
161:         let Some(params) = self.op.params.as_ref() else {
162:             self.param_inputs = vec![];
163:             self.num_params = 0;
164:             return;
165:         };
166: 
167:         self.num_params = params.len();
168:         self.param_inputs = (0..params.len()).map(Some).collect();
169:     }

1: # Welcome to the tket2 development guide <!-- omit in toc -->
2: 
3: This guide is intended to help you get started with developing tket2.
4: 
5: If you find any errors or omissions in this document, please [open an issue](https://github.com/CQCL-DEV/tket2/issues/new)!
6: 
7: ## #️⃣ Setting up the development environment
8: 
9: You can setup the development environment in two ways:
10: 
11: ### The Nix way
12: 
13: The easiest way to setup the development environment is to use the provided
14: [`devenv.nix`](devenv.nix) file. This will setup a development shell with all the
15: required dependencies.
16: 
17: To use this, you will need to install [devenv](https://devenv.sh/getting-started/).
18: Once you have it running, open a shell with:
19: 
20: ```bash
21: devenv shell
22: ```
23: 
24: All the required dependencies should be available. You can automate loading the
25: shell by setting up [direnv](https://devenv.sh/automatic-shell-activation/).
26: 
27: ### Poetry setup
28: 
29: To setup the environment manually you will need:
30: 
31: - Rust 1.75+: https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install
32: 
33: - Poetry: https://python-poetry.org/
34: 
35: 
36: Simply run `poetry shell` to activate an environment with all the required dependencies.
37: 
38: ## 🏃 Running the tests
39: 
40: The repository root contains a Justfile with the most common development tasks.
41: Run `just` to see a list.
42: 
43: To manually compile and test the rust code, run:
44: 
45: ```bash
46: cargo test
47: ```
48: 
49: Run the benchmarks with:
50: 
51: ```bash
52: cargo bench
53: ```
54: 
55: Finally, if you have rust nightly installed, you can run `miri` to detect
56: undefined behaviour in the code. Note that the _devenv_ shell only has rust
57: stable available.
58: 
59: ```bash
60: cargo +nightly miri test
61: ```
62: 
63: To run the python tests, run:
64: 
65: ```bash
66: maturin develop
67: pytest
68: ```
69: 
70: You can use the script in [`.github/pre-commit`](.github/pre-commit) to run the test and formatting required by our CI.
71: To automatically check that before each commit, install it as a hook with:
72: 
73: ```bash
74: ln -s .github/pre-commit $PWD/.git/hooks/pre-commit
75: # Or, to check before pushing instead
76: ln -s .github/pre-commit $PWD/.git/hooks/pre-push
77: ```
78: 
79: ## 💅 Coding Style
80: 
81: The rustfmt tool is used to enforce a consistent rust coding style. The CI will fail if the code is not formatted correctly. Python code is formatted with black.
82: 
83: To format your code, run:
84: 
85: ```bash
86: # Format rust code
87: cargo fmt
88: # Format python code
89: ruff format .
90: ```
91: 
92: We also check for clippy warnings, which are a set of linting rules for rust. To run clippy, run:
93: 
94: ```bash
95: cargo clippy --all-targets
96: ```
97: 
98: ## 📈 Code Coverage
99: 
100: We run coverage checks on the CI. Once you submit a PR, you can review the
101: line-by-line coverage report on
102: [codecov](https://app.codecov.io/gh/CQCL/tket2/commits?branch=All%20branches).
103: 
104: To run the rust coverage checks locally, install `cargo-llvm-cov`, generate the report with:
105: ```bash
106: cargo llvm-cov --lcov > lcov.info
107: ```
108: and open it with your favourite coverage viewer. In VSCode, you can use
109: [`coverage-gutters`](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ryanluker.vscode-coverage-gutters).
110: 
111: Similarly, to run the python coverage checks locally, install `pytest-cov` and run:
112: ```bash
113: pytest --cov=./ --cov-report=xml
114: ```
115: 
116: ## 🌐 Contributing to tket2
117: 
118: We welcome contributions to tket2! Please open [an issue](https://github.com/CQCL/tket2/issues/new) or [pull request](https://github.com/CQCL/tket2/compare) if you have any questions or suggestions.
119: 
120: PRs should be made against the `main` branch, and should pass all CI checks before being merged. This includes using the [conventional commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) format for the PR title.
121: 
122: The general format of a contribution title should be:
123: 
124: ```
125: <type>(<scope>)!: <description>
126: ```
127: 
128: Where the scope is optional, and the `!` is only included if this is a semver breaking change that requires a major version bump.
129: 
130: We accept the following contribution types:
131: 
132: - feat: New features.
133: - fix: Bug fixes.
134: - docs: Improvements to the documentation.
135: - style: Formatting, missing semi colons, etc; no code change.
136: - refactor: Refactoring code without changing behaviour.
137: - perf: Code refactoring focused on improving performance.
138: - test: Adding missing tests, refactoring tests; no production code change.
139: - ci: CI related changes. These changes are not published in the changelog.
140: - chore: Updating build tasks, package manager configs, etc. These changes are not published in the changelog.
141: - revert: Reverting previous commits.

1: # Representation of quantum types in HUGR
2: 
3: TKET2 makes use of the
4: [HUGR](https://github.com/CQCL/hugr/blob/main/specification/hugr.md)
5: IR to represent programs. Here we describe how quantum operations (and
6: the angles associated with some of them) are represented.
7: 
8: Besides a range of quantum operations (like Hadamard, CX, etc.)
9: that take and return `Qubit`, we note the following operations for
10: allocating/deallocating `Qubit`s:
11: 
12: ```
13: qalloc: () -> Qubit
14: qfree: Qubit -> ()
15: ```
16: 
17: `qalloc` allocates a fresh, 0 state Qubit - if none is available at
18: runtime it panics. `qfree` loses a handle to a Qubit (may be reallocated
19: in future). The point at which an allocated qubit is reset may be
20: target/compiler specific.
21: 
22: Note there are also `measurez: Qubit -> (i1, Qubit)` and on supported
23: targets `reset: Qubit -> Qubit` operations to measure or reset a qubit
24: without losing a handle to it.
25: 
26: ## Dynamic vs static allocation
27: 
28: With these operations the programmer/front-end can request dynamic qubit
29: allocation, and the compiler can add/remove/move these operations to use
30: more or fewer qubits. In some use cases, that may not be desirable, and
31: we may instead want to guarantee only a certain number of qubits are
32: used by the program. For this purpose TKET2 places additional
33: constraints on the HUGR that are in line with TKET1 backwards
34: compatibility:
35: 
36: 1. The `main` function takes one `Array<N, Qubit>`
37: input and has one output of the same type (the same statically known
38: size).
39: 2. All Operations that have a `FunctionType` involving `Qubit` have as
40:  many `Qubit` input wires as output.
41: 
42: 
43: With these constraints, we can treat all `Qubit` operations as returning all qubits they take
44: in. The implicit bijection from input `Qubit` to output allows register
45: allocation for all `Qubit` wires. 
46: If further the program does not contain any `qalloc` or `qfree`
47: operations we can state the program only uses `N` qubits.
48: 
49: ## Angles
50: 
51: The "angle" extension defines a specialized `angle<N>` type which is used
52: to express parameters of rotation gates. The type is parametrized by the
53: _log-denominator_, which is an integer $N \in [0, 53]$; angles with
54: log-denominator $N$ are multiples of $2 \pi / 2^N$, where the multiplier is an
55: unsigned `int<N>` in the range $[0, 2^N]$. The maximum log-denominator $53$
56: effectively gives the resolution of a `float64` value; but note that unlike
57: `float64` all angle values are equatable and hashable; and two `angle<N>` that
58: differ by a multiple of $2 \pi$ are _equal_.
59: 
60: The following operations are defined:
61: 
62: | Name           | Inputs     | Outputs    | Meaning |
63: | -------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ------- |
64: | `aconst<N, x>` | none       | `angle<N>` | const node producing angle $2 \pi x / 2^N$ (where $0 \leq x \lt 2^N$) |
65: | `atrunc<M,N>`  | `angle<M>` | `angle<N>` | round `angle<M>` to `angle<N>`, where $M \geq N$, rounding down in $[0, 2\pi)$ if necessary |
66: | `aconvert<M,N>`  | `angle<M>` | `Sum(angle<N>, ErrorType)` | convert `angle<M>` to `angle<N>`, returning an error if $M \gt N$ and exact conversion is impossible |
67: | `aadd<M,N>`    | `angle<M>`, `angle<N>` | `angle<max(M,N)>` | add two angles |
68: | `asub<M,N>`    | `angle<M>`, `angle<N>` | `angle<max(M,N)>` | subtract the second angle from the first |
69: | `aneg<N>`      | `angle<N>` | `angle<N>` | negate an angle |

27: /// The state of an in-progress [`DFGBuilder`] being built from a [`SerialCircuit`].
28: ///
29: /// Mostly used to define helper internal methods.
30: #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
31: pub(super) struct JsonDecoder {
32:     /// The Hugr being built.
33:     pub hugr: DFGBuilder<Hugr>,
34:     /// The dangling wires of the builder.
35:     /// Used to generate [`CircuitBuilder`]s.
36:     dangling_wires: Vec<Wire>,
37:     /// A map from the json registers to flat wire indices.
38:     register_wire: HashMap<RegisterHash, usize>,
39:     /// The number of qubits in the circuit.
40:     num_qubits: usize,
41:     /// The number of bits in the circuit.
42:     num_bits: usize,
43: }
44: 
45: impl JsonDecoder {
46:     /// Initialize a new [`JsonDecoder`], using the metadata from a [`SerialCircuit`].
47:     pub fn new(serialcirc: &SerialCircuit) -> Self {
48:         let num_qubits = serialcirc.qubits.len();
49:         let num_bits = serialcirc.bits.len();
50: 
51:         // Map each (register name, index) pair to an offset in the signature.
52:         let mut wire_map: HashMap<RegisterHash, usize> =
53:             HashMap::with_capacity(num_bits + num_qubits);
54:         for (i, register) in serialcirc
55:             .qubits
56:             .iter()
57:             .chain(serialcirc.bits.iter())
58:             .enumerate()
59:         {
60:             if register.1.len() != 1 {
61:                 // TODO: Support multi-index registers?
62:                 panic!("Register {} has more than one index", register.0);
63:             }
64:             wire_map.insert((register, 0).into(), i);
65:         }
66:         let sig = FunctionType::new_endo(
67:             [vec![QB_T; num_qubits], vec![LINEAR_BIT.clone(); num_bits]].concat(),
68:         );
69:         // .with_extension_delta(&ExtensionSet::singleton(&TKET1_EXTENSION_ID));
70: 
71:         let mut dfg = DFGBuilder::new(sig).unwrap();
72: 
73:         // Metadata. The circuit requires "name", and we store other things that
74:         // should pass through the serialization roundtrip.
75:         dfg.set_metadata("name", json!(serialcirc.name));
76:         dfg.set_metadata(METADATA_PHASE, json!(serialcirc.phase));
77:         dfg.set_metadata(
78:             METADATA_IMPLICIT_PERM,
79:             json!(serialcirc.implicit_permutation),
80:         );
81:         dfg.set_metadata(METADATA_Q_REGISTERS, json!(serialcirc.qubits));
82:         dfg.set_metadata(METADATA_B_REGISTERS, json!(serialcirc.bits));
83: 
84:         let dangling_wires = dfg.input_wires().collect::<Vec<_>>();
85:         JsonDecoder {
86:             hugr: dfg,
87:             dangling_wires,
88:             register_wire: wire_map,
89:             num_qubits,
90:             num_bits,
91:         }
92:     }
93: 
94:     /// Finish building the [`Hugr`].
95:     pub fn finish(self) -> Hugr {
96:         // TODO: Throw validation error?
97:         self.hugr
98:             .finish_hugr_with_outputs(self.dangling_wires, &REGISTRY)
99:             .unwrap()
100:     }
101: 
102:     /// Add a [`Command`] from the serial circuit to the [`JsonDecoder`].
103:     ///
104:     /// - [`Command`]: circuit_json::Command
105:     pub fn add_command(&mut self, command: circuit_json::Command) {
106:         // TODO Store the command's `opgroup` in the metadata.
107:         let circuit_json::Command { op, args, .. } = command;
108:         let num_qubits = args
109:             .iter()
110:             .take_while(|&arg| self.reg_wire(arg, 0) < self.num_qubits)
111:             .count();
112:         let num_bits = args.len() - num_qubits;
113:         let op = JsonOp::new_from_op(op, num_qubits, num_bits);
114: 
115:         let args: Vec<_> = args.into_iter().map(|reg| self.reg_wire(&reg, 0)).collect();
116: 
117:         let param_wires: Vec<Wire> = op
118:             .param_inputs()
119:             .map(|p| self.create_param_wire(p))
120:             .collect();
121: 
122:         let append_wires = args
123:             .into_iter()
124:             .map(CircuitUnit::Linear)
125:             .chain(param_wires.into_iter().map(CircuitUnit::Wire));
126: 
127:         self.with_circ_builder(|circ| {
128:             circ.append_and_consume(&op, append_wires).unwrap();
129:         });
130:     }
131: 
132:     /// Apply a function to the internal hugr builder viewed as a [`CircuitBuilder`].
133:     fn with_circ_builder(&mut self, f: impl FnOnce(&mut CircuitBuilder<DFGBuilder<Hugr>>)) {
134:         let mut circ = self.hugr.as_circuit(mem::take(&mut self.dangling_wires));
135:         f(&mut circ);
136:         self.dangling_wires = circ.finish();
137:     }
138: 
139:     /// Returns the wire carrying a parameter.
140:     ///
141:     /// If the parameter is a constant, a constant definition is added to the Hugr.
142:     ///
143:     /// TODO: If the parameter is a variable, returns the corresponding wire from the input.
144:     fn create_param_wire(&mut self, param: &str) -> Wire {
145:         match try_param_to_constant(param) {
146:             Some(c) => {
147:                 let const_type = FLOAT64_TYPE;
148:                 let const_op = Const::new(c, const_type).unwrap();
149:                 self.hugr.add_load_const(const_op).unwrap()
150:             }
151:             None => {
152:                 // store string in custom op.
153:                 let symb_op = symbolic_constant_op(param);
154:                 let o = self.hugr.add_dataflow_op(symb_op, []).unwrap();
155:                 o.out_wire(0)
156:             }
157:         }
158:     }
159: 
160:     /// Return the wire index for the `elem`th value of a given register.
161:     ///
162:     /// Relies on TKET1 constraint that all registers have unique names.
163:     fn reg_wire(&self, register: &circuit_json::Register, elem: usize) -> usize {
164:         self.register_wire[&(register, elem).into()]
165:     }
166: }
167: 
168: /// A hashed register, used to identify registers in the [`JsonDecoder::register_wire`] map,
169: /// avoiding string clones on lookup.
170: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
171: struct RegisterHash {
172:     hash: u64,
173: }
174: 
175: impl From<(&circuit_json::Register, usize)> for RegisterHash {
176:     fn from((reg, elem): (&circuit_json::Register, usize)) -> Self {
177:         let mut hasher = DefaultHasher::new();
178:         reg.0.hash(&mut hasher);
179:         reg.1[elem].hash(&mut hasher);
180:         Self {
181:             hash: hasher.finish(),
182:         }
183:     }
184: }

4: //! [`LinearUnit`]), or a wire between two HUGR nodes (a [`Wire`]).

8: //! applied.

111:     // new unit ids sequentially.

113:     pub(super) fn new(

116:         direction: Direction,
117:         unit_labeller: UL,

129:     /// Initialize the boundary types.
130:     ///
131:     /// We use a [`TypeRow`] to avoid allocating for simple boundaries, but if
132:     /// any static port is present we create a new owned [`TypeRow`] with them included.
133:     //

135:     // We should revisit it once this is reworked on the HUGR side.
136:     fn init_types(circuit: &impl Circuit, node: Node, direction: Direction) -> TypeRow {
137:         let optype = circuit.get_optype(node);
138:         let sig = circuit.signature(node).unwrap_or_default();
139:         let mut types = match direction {
140:             Direction::Outgoing => sig.output,
141:             Direction::Incoming => sig.input,
142:         };
143:         if let Some(EdgeKind::Static(static_type)) = optype.static_port_kind(direction) {
144:             types.to_mut().push(static_type);
145:         };
146:         if let Some(EdgeKind::Static(other)) = optype.other_port_kind(direction) {
147:             types.to_mut().push(other);
148:         }
149:         types
150:     }

152:     /// Construct an output value to yield.
153:     ///
154:     /// Calls [`UnitLabeller::assign_linear`] to assign a linear unit id to the linear ports.
155:     /// Non-linear ports are assigned [`CircuitUnit::Wire`]s via [`UnitLabeller::assign_wire`].
156:     #[inline]
157:     fn make_value(&self, typ: &Type, port: Port) -> Option<(CircuitUnit, Port, Type)> {
158:         let unit = if type_is_linear(typ) {
159:             let linear_unit =
160:                 self.unit_labeller
161:                     .assign_linear(self.node, port, self.linear_count - 1);
162:             CircuitUnit::Linear(linear_unit.index())
163:         } else {
164:             let wire = self.unit_labeller.assign_wire(self.node, port)?;
165:             CircuitUnit::Wire(wire)
166:         };

168:     }

182:             self.pos += 1;
183:             if type_is_linear(typ) {

# tket2

[![build_status][]](https://github.com/CQCL-DEV/tket2/actions)
![msrv][]
[![codecov][]](https://codecov.io/gh/CQCL/tket2)

Version 2 of the TKET compiler: an open source quantum compiler developed by
Quantinuum. Central to TKET2's design is its hardware agnosticism, which allows
researchers and quantum software developers to take advantage of its state of
the art compilation for many different quantum architectures.

TKET2 represents quantum circuits using the [HUGR][] intermediate
representation. This repository provides the Rust crates that implement the
compiler, as well as Python bindings and command line tools built on top of it.

  [build_status]: https://github.com/CQCL-DEV/hugr/workflows/Continuous%20integration/badge.svg?branch=main
  [msrv]: https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.75.0%2B-blue.svg
  [codecov]: https://img.shields.io/codecov/c/gh/CQCL/tket2?logo=codecov

## What can you do with tket2?

- **Model circuits.** TKET2 circuits are [HUGR][] programs. The
  [`Circuit` trait][Circuit] provides a common interface to query a circuit's
  qubit and gate counts and iterate over its operations as
  [`Command`s][Command].
- **Describe quantum operations.** The [`Tk2Op`][Tk2Op] enum bundles common
  quantum operations (H, CX, T, measurement, qubit allocation/reset, ...) as
  part of the TKET2 HUGR extension.
- **Rewrite circuits.** Subcircuits can be extracted as
  [`Subcircuit`][Subcircuit]s and replaced with equivalent circuits via
  [`CircuitRewrite`][CircuitRewrite]s. Different [`Rewriter`][Rewriter]s find
  the rewrite rules a circuit matches, and rewrites are applied according to a
  [`RewriteStrategy`][RewriteStrategy] (greedy, exhaustive, or threshold-based).
- **Optimise circuits.** The [`BadgerOptimiser`][BadgerOptimiser] repeatedly
  searches a space of equivalent circuits to find the lowest-cost version of an
  input circuit. Circuits can also be split into independently optimisable
  [`CircuitChunks`][CircuitChunks].
- **Interoperate with TKET1.** Circuits can be loaded from, and saved to, the
  TKET1 JSON serialization format through the `load_tk1_json_*` and
  `save_tk1_json_*` functions, so existing TKET1 workflows can drive the TKET2
  backend.

## Getting started

Add `tket2` and `hugr` to your dependencies:

```toml
[dependencies]
tket2 = "0.0.0-alpha.1"
hugr = "0.2.0"
```

The simplest way to get started is to load a TKET1 circuit from its JSON
serialization and inspect it with the [`Circuit`][Circuit] interface:

```rust
use tket2::json::load_tk1_json_str;
use tket2::{op_matches, Circuit, Tk2Op};

fn main() {
    let circ = load_tk1_json_str(
        r#"{
            "phase": "0",
            "bits": [],
            "qubits": [["q", [0]]],
            "commands": [
                {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "H"}},
                {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "T"}}
            ],
            "implicit_permutation": [[["q", [0]], ["q", [0]]]]
        }"#,
    )
    .expect("Failed to parse circuit");

    assert_eq!(circ.qubit_count(), 1);
    assert_eq!(circ.num_gates(), 2);

    for command in circ.commands() {
        let op = command.optype();
        assert!(op_matches(op, Tk2Op::H) || op_matches(op, Tk2Op::T));
    }
}
```

More documentation is available on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/tket2).

## Features

- `pyo3`
  Enables some python bindings via pyo3. See the `tket2-py` folder for more.

- `portmatching`
  Enables pattern matching using the `portmatching` crate.

- `rewrite-tracing`
  Adds opt-in tracking of the rewrites applied to a circuit.

## Related projects

- [HUGR](https://github.com/CQCL/hugr): the intermediate representation used by
  TKET2. Quantum programs, their extensions and the rewrite rules applied by
  TKET2 are all described as HUGR programs.
- [TKET](https://www.quantinuum.com/products-solutions/tket): the first version
  of the TKET compiler, whose JSON serialization format is used for
  interoperability.

## Developing TKET2

See [DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md) for instructions on setting up the development environment.

## License

This project is licensed under Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE][] or http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0).

  [LICENSE]: LICENCE
  [HUGR]: https://github.com/CQCL/hugr
  [Circuit]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/trait.Circuit.html
  [Command]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/struct.Command.html
  [Tk2Op]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/enum.Tk2Op.html
  [Subcircuit]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/struct.Subcircuit.html
  [CircuitRewrite]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/struct.CircuitRewrite.html
  [Rewriter]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/trait.Rewriter.html
  [RewriteStrategy]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/rewrite/strategy/trait.RewriteStrategy.html
  [BadgerOptimiser]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/optimiser/badger/struct.BadgerOptimiser.html
  [CircuitChunks]: https://docs.rs/tket2/latest/tket2/struct.CircuitChunks.html

+//! operations that have no direct representation are embedded as opaque

+//! ## Rewriting
+//!
+//! TKET2's circuit optimisation is based on rewriting subcircuits by equivalent
+//! ones:
+//!
+//! - A part of a circuit can be extracted as a [`Subcircuit`], and used to
+//!   define a [`CircuitRewrite`] that replaces it with another circuit.
+//! - Different [`Rewriter`]s search a circuit for the rewrite rules it matches.
+//! - Rewrites are applied according to a

+//! - [`CircuitChunks`] can be used to split a circuit into pieces that can be
+//!   optimised independently and later reassembled.

+//! lexicographic combinations of cost functions (see [`LexicographicCost`]).
+//!
+//! ## Optimising
+//!
+//! The [`BadgerOptimiser`][optimiser::badger::BadgerOptimiser] is an
+//! optimisation loop that repeatedly uses a rewriter and a rewrite strategy to
+//! search for lower-cost versions of a circuit, keeping the best candidates in
+//! a priority queue.

+//! the greedy commutation-based [`apply_greedy_commutation`][passes].

1: //! # TKET2: The Hardware Agnostic Quantum Compiler
2: //!
3: //! TKET2 is an open source quantum compiler developed by Quantinuum. Central to
4: //! TKET2's design is its hardware agnosticism, which allows researchers and
5: //! quantum software developers to take advantage of its state of the art
6: //! compilation for many different quantum architectures.
7: //!
8: //! Circuits are represented as [HUGR][] programs. This crate provides a set of
9: //! tools to build, inspect, rewrite and optimise quantum circuits, and to
10: //! interoperate with the TKET1 JSON serialization format.
11: //!
12: //! ## Circuits
13: //!
14: //! The [`Circuit`] trait defines a common interface over any HUGR structure
15: //! that describes a circuit. It provides methods to query the circuit's
16: //! signature, qubit and gate counts, and to iterate over its gates as
17: //! [`Command`]s (an operation applied to a specific set of wires).
18: //!
19: //! The [`Hugr`] type is the concrete circuit representation used throughout
20: //! this crate.
21: //!
22: //! ## Operations
23: //!
24: //! Common quantum operations are defined in the [`Tk2Op`] enum, covering
25: //! single-qubit and multi-qubit gates as well as measurement, reset and qubit
26: //! allocation and deallocation. When read from a serialized TKET1 circuit,
27: //! operations that have no direct representation are embedded as opaque
28: //! operations from the TKET1 extension.
29: //!
30: //! [`op_matches`] can be used to check whether an [`OpType`][hugr::ops::OpType]
31: //! corresponds to a given TKET2 operation.
32: //!
33: //! ## Rewriting
34: //!
35: //! TKET2's circuit optimisation is based on rewriting subcircuits by equivalent
36: //! ones:
37: //!
38: //! - A part of a circuit can be extracted as a [`Subcircuit`], and used to
39: //!   define a [`CircuitRewrite`] that replaces it with another circuit.
40: //! - Different [`Rewriter`]s search a circuit for the rewrite rules it matches.
41: //! - Rewrites are applied according to a
42: //!   [`RewriteStrategy`][rewrite::strategy::RewriteStrategy], such as the
43: //!   greedy [`GreedyRewriteStrategy`][rewrite::strategy::GreedyRewriteStrategy]
44: //!   or the exhaustive strategies in [`rewrite::strategy`].
45: //! - [`CircuitChunks`] can be used to split a circuit into pieces that can be
46: //!   optimised independently and later reassembled.
47: //!
48: //! Rewrites can be assigned a [`CircuitCost`], and circuits ordered by
49: //! lexicographic combinations of cost functions (see [`LexicographicCost`]).
50: //!
51: //! ## Optimising
52: //!
53: //! The [`BadgerOptimiser`][optimiser::badger::BadgerOptimiser] is an
54: //! optimisation loop that repeatedly uses a rewriter and a rewrite strategy to
55: //! search for lower-cost versions of a circuit, keeping the best candidates in
56: //! a priority queue.
57: //!
58: //! [`passes`] contains higher-level circuit transforms and utilities, including
59: //! the greedy commutation-based [`apply_greedy_commutation`][passes].
60: //!
61: //! ## Serialization
62: //!
63: //! Circuits can be loaded from, and saved to, the TKET1 JSON format using the
64: //! [`load_tk1_json_str`]/[`load_tk1_json_file`] and
65: //! [`save_tk1_json_str`]/[`save_tk1_json_file`] functions.
66: //!
67: //! ## Feature flags
68: //!
69: //! - `pyo3`: Enables some Python bindings via [pyo3](https://pyo3.rs/). See
70: //!   the `tket2-py` folder for more.
71: //! - `portmatching`: Enables pattern matching using the `portmatching` crate.
72: //!   This is required for the [`ECCRewriter`][rewrite::ecc_rewriter::ECCRewriter]
73: //!   and the [`portmatching`] module.
74: //! - `rewrite-tracing`: Adds opt-in tracking of the rewrites applied to a
75: //!   circuit.
76: //!
77: //! ## Example
78: //!
79: //! The simplest way to get started is to load a TKET1 circuit from its JSON
80: //! serialization, and inspect it using the [`Circuit`] interface:
81: //!
82: //! ```
83: //! use tket2::{load_tk1_json_str, op_matches, Circuit, Tk2Op};
84: //!
85: //! let circ = load_tk1_json_str(
86: //!     r#"{
87: //!         "phase": "0",
88: //!         "bits": [],
89: //!         "qubits": [["q", [0]]],
90: //!         "commands": [
91: //!             {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "H"}},
92: //!             {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "T"}}
93: //!         ],
94: //!         "implicit_permutation": [[["q", [0]], ["q", [0]]]]
95: //!     }"#,
96: //! )
97: //! .unwrap();
98: //!
99: //! assert_eq!(circ.qubit_count(), 1);
100: //! assert_eq!(circ.num_gates(), 2);
101: //!
102: //! // Every command in the circuit is one of the TKET2 operations we loaded.
103: //! for command in circ.commands() {
104: //!     let op = command.optype();
105: //!     assert!(op_matches(op, Tk2Op::H) || op_matches(op, Tk2Op::T));
106: //! }
107: //! ```
108: //!
109: //! [HUGR]: https://github.com/CQCL/hugr
110:

112: pub mod extension;
113: pub mod json;
114: pub(crate) mod ops;
115: pub mod optimiser;

20: ## What can you do with tket2?
21: 
22: - **Model circuits.** TKET2 circuits are [HUGR][] programs. The
23:   [`Circuit` trait][Circuit] provides a common interface to query a circuit's
24:   qubit and gate counts and iterate over its operations as
25:   [`Command`s][Command].
26: - **Describe quantum operations.** The [`Tk2Op`][Tk2Op] enum bundles common
27:   quantum operations (H, CX, T, measurement, qubit allocation/reset, ...) as
28:   part of the TKET2 HUGR extension.
29: - **Rewrite circuits.** Subcircuits can be extracted as
30:   [`Subcircuit`][Subcircuit]s and replaced with equivalent circuits via
31:   [`CircuitRewrite`][CircuitRewrite]s. Different [`Rewriter`][Rewriter]s find
32:   the rewrite rules a circuit matches, and rewrites are applied according to a
33:   [`RewriteStrategy`][RewriteStrategy] (greedy, exhaustive, or threshold-based).
34: - **Optimise circuits.** The [`BadgerOptimiser`][BadgerOptimiser] repeatedly
35:   searches a space of equivalent circuits to find the lowest-cost version of an
36:   input circuit. Circuits can also be split into independently optimisable
37:   [`CircuitChunks`][CircuitChunks].
38: - **Interoperate with TKET1.** Circuits can be loaded from, and saved to, the
39:   TKET1 JSON serialization format through the `load_tk1_json_*` and
40:   `save_tk1_json_*` functions, so existing TKET1 workflows can drive the TKET2
41:   backend.
42: 
43: ## Getting started
44: 
45: Add `tket2` and `quantinuum-hugr` to your dependencies:
46: 
47: ```toml
48: [dependencies]
49: tket2 = "0.0.0-alpha.1"
50: quantinuum-hugr = { git = "https://github.com/CQCL/hugr", tag = "v0.2.0" }
51: ```
52: 
53: The simplest way to get started is to load a TKET1 circuit from its JSON
54: serialization and inspect it with the [`Circuit`][Circuit] interface:
55: 
56: ```rust
57: use tket2::{load_tk1_json_str, op_matches, Circuit, Tk2Op};
58: 
59: fn main() {
60:     let circ = load_tk1_json_str(
61:         r#"{
62:             "phase": "0",
63:             "bits": [],
64:             "qubits": [["q", [0]]],
65:             "commands": [
66:                 {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "H"}},
67:                 {"args": [["q", [0]]], "op": {"type": "T"}}
68:             ],
69:             "implicit_permutation": [[["q", [0]], ["q", [0]]]]
70:         }"#,
